nodes.title: Keep the column apart from the tile
nodes.why: Focus stores the column the user chose with Left and Right, and each row shows the nearest tile it has. Passing through a two-tile row clamps what is shown, not what is kept, so the next long row lands back in the chosen column.
nodes.alternative: Store the focused tile index and clamp it on every move.
nodes.tradeoff: One number is simpler, but a short row overwrites it: after Documentaries, every row below starts from its second tile.

nodes.title: Work out what is in view from focus
nodes.why: The TV's browser has no IntersectionObserver, and on a TV the screen moves only when focus does, so focus is the best guide to what the user sees next. The focused row and the two below it form a prefetch window: their sets start loading before focus gets there, and a row that is still loading when focus arrives shows its placeholder.
nodes.alternative: Measure the rows with getBoundingClientRect when the page scrolls.
nodes.tradeoff: It needs no IntersectionObserver either, but it reads layout on every scroll, which is slow on a TV processor, and it adds nothing focus does not already say.

nodes.title: Ask for each set once
nodes.why: A set is marked as requested before its answer arrives, so moving away and back while it loads does not ask again. The mark lives in a ref because it never changes what is drawn.
nodes.alternative: Request a set whenever its row is in view and its titles are missing.
nodes.tradeoff: That reads naturally, but every Up or Down press that keeps the row in view during the 600 ms wait sends another request for the same set.

nodes.title: Derive one focus target and move DOM focus to it
nodes.why: Every way focus can change, a key press, a set arriving or the details opening and closing, ends in one focus target that names the element to focus. One effect moves DOM focus when that target changes, so a placeholder hands focus to its tile the moment the titles render, and each key press puts DOM focus back on the target if a click took it away.
nodes.alternative: Call focus() from each key handler.
nodes.tradeoff: It moves focus at once, but a row that finishes loading later has no handler to move focus into it, and each handler repeats the lookup.

nodes.title: Let a loading row hold focus
nodes.why: Pressing Down onto a row that is still loading moves focus to its placeholder, so the remote always does something visible. When the titles arrive the target becomes the tile at the kept column, and only if focus is still on that row.
nodes.alternative: Ignore Down until the row below has loaded.
nodes.tradeoff: Focus never lands on an empty row, but a press that does nothing feels broken on a TV, where users cannot see why.

nodes.title: Keep the remote inside the details
nodes.why: While the details are open, the key handler returns before the row logic, so no arrow moves the focus state of the rows behind, and the focus key names a details button. Only Left and Right move, between the two buttons.
nodes.alternative: Mark the rows inert while the details are open.
nodes.tradeoff: inert keeps clicks and Tab out of the rows in a modern browser, but an old TV browser may not support it, and a key listener on window receives the arrows either way, so the handler has to ignore them anyway.

nodes.title: Use buttons for tiles
nodes.why: A button takes focus and turns Enter into a click by itself, so the tile opens its details without an Enter handler, and the same button works with a mouse in the preview.
nodes.alternative: Use a focusable div and handle Enter in the key handler.
nodes.tradeoff: It works when the key handler opens the details on Enter, but screen readers do not announce the div as something to press.

nodes.title: Show the name when the artwork fails
nodes.why: An image that fails fires error on its img element. The tile then swaps the image for the title's name, so the row has no blank tile and the title can still be found and opened.
nodes.alternative: Hide the broken image and leave the tile empty.
nodes.tradeoff: Simpler, but an empty card on a TV gives no hint what it is.

nodes.title: Return focus to the tile on Back
nodes.why: Closing the details only clears them; focus still names the tile that opened them, so the focus effect moves DOM focus back to it and the next arrow continues from there.
nodes.alternative: Remember the opening element in a ref and focus it on close.
nodes.tradeoff: That also works, but it keeps a second record of where focus is, which can disagree with the first.
